name: metal-json
workload: Parsing twitter-shaped JSON documents (and canada.json/citm_catalog.json) at sizes from 0.6 MiB to 512 MiB on an Apple Silicon GPU (Metal compute kernels) vs CPU simdjson, both producing bit-identical simdjson-format tapes.
claimed_speedup: 1.34x-2.71x faster than simdjson on documents >= 8 MiB (2.06x-2.71x on 100-512 MiB); loses to simdjson below the ~4.3 MiB crossover (as low as 0.12x, i.e. ~8x slower, at 0.6 MiB)
compiler_and_flags: simdjson v4.6.4 built with -O3 -mcpu=native; metal-json is Rust + Metal shaders, Criterion for timing
hardware: Apple M5 Max, 128 GiB unified memory, macOS 26.5.1
tradeoffs: GPU dispatch/sync overhead makes it far slower than simdjson on small documents; Apple Silicon/Metal + unified-memory specific, not portable to other GPUs or discrete-GPU systems; adds a GPU dependency and complexity a pure-CPU parser doesn't need.
caveats: Single-machine, single-vendor benchmark (one Apple M5 Max); crossover point (~4.3 MiB) is dataset-shape dependent per the author's own admission (canada.json crosses over near 2.1 MiB, citm_catalog still favors simdjson at 1.6 MiB); compares only the simdjson stage-1/tape build, not a full application parse+access path; very new project (18 stars, first commits this month).
found_via: Blogs / talks: gh search code "faster than simdjson" -> Brooooooklyn/metal-json docs/parsing-json-on-an-apple-gpu.md

name: reflect-cpp
workload: JSON read/write (serialize/deserialize) of canada.json (float-heavy), licenses.json (nested, string-heavy), and a small 'person' struct, via continuous Google Benchmark runs in CI.
claimed_speedup: ~10x faster than nlohmann/json; consistently ~2x faster than RapidJSON; slightly slower than simdjson and yyjson
compiler_and_flags: gcc 11.4 on Ubuntu 22.4, CMake Release build (-DREFLECTCPP_BUILD_BENCHMARKS=ON), Google Benchmark
hardware: GitHub Actions Ubuntu runner (specific CPU model not stated in the benchmark doc)
tradeoffs: reflect-cpp's JSON backend is built on top of yyjson, so most of the raw speed comes from that dependency rather than novel parsing code; requires compile-time struct reflection instead of a dynamic DOM like nlohmann/json, so it targets a narrower use case (known-schema structs, not arbitrary JSON).
caveats: CPU model for the numbers is never stated (only 'gcc 11.4 on Ubuntu 22.4'), which caps the tier below A despite public, continuously-run benchmark code; the numeric results are shown as bar-chart PNGs referenced from the doc, not raw tables, so exact ratios beyond the stated '~10x' / '~2x' summary could not be independently re-derived from text.
found_via: Blogs / talks: gh search code "faster than nlohmann" -> getml/reflect-cpp docs/benchmarks.md and benchmarks/README.md

name: libJSON (IgnacioPomar)
workload: Read (parse + walk full DOM) and write (build DOM + serialize) of random-walk OHLC minute-candle JSON at three sizes (10, 1,440 and 10,080 candles), minimum time over 30 rounds.
claimed_speedup: Read faster than nlohmann/json at every size tested: ~1.25x (small, 21.1us vs 26.4us), ~1.42x (medium, 2632.2us vs 3737.0us), ~1.38x (large, 19772.3us vs 27254.9us) (derived from page data); loses on write, and loses to RapidJSON/simdjson/glaze on both read and write
tradeoffs: Every JSON node is its own heap allocation via shared_ptr (one make_shared per value), making it the slowest of the four libraries tested at writing; author explicitly built it as a C++17/shared_ptr learning exercise, not for production use; loses to RapidJSON, simdjson and glaze on every measured workload and only beats nlohmann/json.
caveats: Self-described 'learning project' by a solo author, 0 stars; no CPU model or compiler flags stated for the numbers; the benchmark README is written in Spanish; the author states he would pick glaze or RapidJSON over his own library in practice; the win margin over nlohmann/json (1.25x-1.42x) is modest compared to the much larger gaps to RapidJSON/simdjson. Public-domain Unlicense dedication: no patent grant.
found_via: Blogs / talks: gh search code "faster than nlohmann" -> IgnacioPomar/libJSON README.md and benchmarks/README.md

name: libjson (xnacly)
workload: Parsing JSON of varying complexity (naive, string-escape-heavy, deeply-nested 'hard' cases) via Go micro-benchmarks, plus parsing generated 1MB-100MB JSON files as a CLI end-to-end benchmark.
claimed_speedup: 1.94x-2.43x faster in Go benchmarks (ns/op) with 2.1x-3.1x fewer allocations; 1.69x-1.81x faster wall-clock time on 1MB-100MB files
compiler_and_flags: go test -bench=. -benchmem, default Go toolchain build flags
tradeoffs: Zero-copy design mutates the input byte slice in place for string unescaping, so callers cannot reuse/read the original buffer after parsing; uses a custom JIT-cached query language instead of encoding/json's reflection-based struct tags, so migration requires API changes; very new, low-adoption project.
caveats: Very small project (5 stars, single author); the 'Naive'/'Escaped'/'Hard' benchmark categories are self-defined test cases within the repo rather than a standard external corpus; last commit is a few months old but still within the 'active' 12-month window.
found_via: Blogs / talks: gh search code "faster than encoding/json" -> xnacly/libjson README.md

name: FastestJSONInTheWest
workload: End-to-end parse of small/medium/large JSON payloads (162B-1MB), plus post-parse field access, array iteration over 10K records, and on-demand single-field extraction from a 1MB payload, via Google Benchmark.
claimed_speedup: Loses badly on raw parse (simdjson is 46x-116x faster, e.g. 83-112 MB/s vs 4.1-11.1 GB/s); wins on pre-parsed field access (1.26x) and array iteration (2.24x); its own on-demand mode is 7.8x faster than its own full parse for single-field extraction, but this is a self-comparison, not a win over simdjson's ondemand mode
tradeoffs: Raw parse throughput is 46x-116x slower than simdjson; the claimed wins are limited to secondary access patterns on an already-built DOM (repeated field access, array iteration) rather than parse-from-bytes speed, which is the primary thing simdjson is used for; also supports read-write serialization which simdjson does not, so that part of the comparison isn't head-to-head.
caveats: Solo, unverified project with 0 stars and a very sprawling repo layout (Bazel, ai/, python bindings, many top-level docs) consistent with heavy AI-assisted authoring; GitHub reports the license as 'Other'/NOASSERTION and a LICENSE_BSD_4_CLAUSE file exists but a direct raw-content fetch of a LICENSE file 404'd, so exact terms are unconfirmed (treated as non-OSI/reference); the project's own name overstates the result, since on its core job (parsing from bytes) it is dramatically slower than simdjson; numbers are entirely self-reported with no independent reproduction found.
found_via: Blogs / talks: gh search code "faster than simdjson" -> oldboldpilot/fastestjsoninthewest docs/BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md

name: ffjson
workload: Marshal/unmarshal of a Cloudflare log-line struct (goser benchmark) and a Stripe-Customer-like nested struct (go.stripe benchmark) using Go benchmarks.
claimed_speedup: 1.91x faster than encoding/json on the goser benchmark; 2.11x faster than encoding/json on the go.stripe benchmark
tradeoffs: Requires a code-generation step (the ffjson tool generates MarshalJSON/UnmarshalJSON per struct) instead of runtime reflection, adding a build step and generated-code maintenance burden; larger binary size from generated code.
caveats: Blog post is from 2014 and states no hardware or Go compiler version; the numbers are over a decade old and Go's encoding/json plus compiler have changed substantially since (community discussion elsewhere notes such old 'faster than encoding/json' claims tend to shrink over time); repo has had no commits since 2019 (abandoned), though it remains widely known/vendored historically (2.99k stars).
found_via: Blogs / talks: HN Algolia search "fastest json serialization" -> journal.paul.querna.org/articles/2014/03/31/ffjson-faster-json-in-go/ (redirects to paul.querna.org)

name: zenjson
workload: Parsing and stringifying the nativejson-benchmark corpus (twitter.json, canada.json, citm_catalog.json).
claimed_speedup: Parsing ~2-3.6x faster than RapidJSON (e.g. twitter.json: 2034.7 MB/s vs 570.3 MB/s) and within a few percent to ~1.5x of simdjson depending on file; 10x-27x faster than nlohmann/json. Stringifying ~2.6-3.4x faster than RapidJSON and ~7-9.5x faster than nlohmann/json.
compiler_and_flags: Visual Studio 2017, 64-bit; RapidJSON built with RAPIDJSON_SSE2/ParseInsitu; simdjson compiled with /std:c++17 and allocate_capacity pre-allocation; others default flags
tradeoffs: In-situ parsing modifies and depends on the input buffer (like RapidJSON's insitu mode), so callers lose the original string; single-header and small (<2k LOC) but unmaintained since 2019, so it lacks fixes for JSON edge cases found in the years since.
caveats: No commits since 2019 (abandoned); only 8 stars, effectively unverified independently; benchmark run on a single 2017-era Windows/MSVC machine, no Linux/GCC/Clang numbers given; a benchmark/ directory exists in the repo but I did not execute it myself to reproduce the numbers, only read the reported results.
found_via: Blogs / talks: gh search code "faster than RapidJSON" -> re-esper/zenjson README.md
